sentences.text: Much of the anatomy of Rebbachisaurus garasbae remains unknown because it is known only from a single incomplete skeleton.
Recent estimates suggest Rebbachisaurus was about 14 meters long and weighed between 7 and 12 metric tons.
Rebbachisaurus vertebrae could reach up to 150 cm in height, which is significantly taller than those of South American rebbachisaurids.
Rebbachisaurus is classified as a medium-sized sauropod but represents one of the largest known rebbachisaurids.
The holotype skeleton of Rebbachisaurus was discovered in 1948 in the Errachidia Province of Morocco.
French paleontologist René Lavocat discovered fossils of Rebbachisaurus between October 1948 and April 1949 at the Gara Sbaa locality in Morocco.
René Lavocat formally described and named the species Rebbachisaurus garasbae in 1954.
The holotype specimen was deposited at the National Museum of Natural History in Paris under the number MNHN-MRS 1958 by January 1952.
Rebbachisaurus was the first rebbachisaurid dinosaur to be discovered and named.
Ibiricu and colleagues suggested in 2017 that postcranial skeletal pneumaticity in rebbachisaurids was an adaptation to lower skeletal density.
John Whitlock studied dental microwear on a tooth assigned to Rebbachisaurus in 2011.
Traits of its teeth suggest that Rebbachisaurus was a generalist ground-height browser.
Ibrahim and colleagues suggested in 2020 that Rebbachisaurus likely lacked the self-supporting tooth rows found in Nigersaurus based on wear patterns.
Rebbachisaurus garasbae is the only currently valid species within the genus Rebbachisaurus.
In 2004, Salgado and colleagues reclassified R. tessonei as a separate genus named Limaysaurus.
Rebbachisaurus serves as the type genus for the family Rebbachisauridae and the subfamily Rebbachisaurinae.
Rebbachisaurus lived in Africa during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 99 to 97 million years ago.
Rebbachisaurus lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 99 to 97 million years ago in the Cenomanian stage.
Rebbachisaurus lived in what is now Africa.
Rebbachisaurus lived from the Albian to the Cenomanian, between 106.3 and 93.9 million years ago.
Some researchers have hypothesized that R. tamesnensis is a camarasaurid rather than a diplodocoid or valid species.
It has been hypothesized that R. tamesnensis is a chimera composed of fossils from Jobaria and Nigersaurus.
Wilson and Allain (2015) identified three sacral neural spines as spines 1–3, but this identification was based solely on comparisons with Nigersaurus.
It is debated whether R. tamesnensis is a synonym or a chimera of Nigersaurus taqueti.
